title: Polynomial Rings and Field Extensions
---

Polynomials connect algebra to analysis, number theory and geometry. Given a field $k$, we construct the ring of polynomials $k[x]$, some rings and fields built from it, and we see how to enlarge $k$ so that it contains roots of polynomials.

## <span class="num">4.3.1</span> The Polynomial Ring $k[x]$

:::definition{4.3.1} Polynomial ring
Given a field $k$, the ***polynomial ring in one variable*** over $k$ is $$k[x] \coloneqq \left\{a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_n x^n \;\middle|\; n \in \NN, \, a_i \in k \right\}.$$ Here $x$ is a ***formal variable***: it is not an element of $k$ or of any other set. Formally, a polynomial is a sequence $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots)$ of elements of $k$ with only finitely many nonzero terms. Polynomials are added coefficientwise, and multiplied by expanding and collecting powers of $x$ using $x^i x^j = x^{i+j}$: $$\Big(\sum_i a_i x^i\Big)\Big(\sum_j b_j x^j\Big) = \sum_n c_n x^n, \qquad c_n = \sum_{i + j = n} a_i b_j.$$
:::

Multiplication is *not* coefficientwise: $(1 + x)(1 + x) = 1 + 2x + x^2$. One checks from these formulas that $k[x]$ is a commutative ring with identity the constant polynomial $1$. The only axiom that needs a computation is associativity of multiplication: for $f = \sum a_i x^i$, $g = \sum b_j x^j$ and $h = \sum c_l x^l$, the coefficient of $x^n$ in both $(fg)h$ and $f(gh)$ is $\sum_{i + j + l = n} a_i b_j c_l$. The constants form a subring of $k[x]$ that we identify with $k$.

:::note
The adjective “formal” matters. When we write $x^2 + 1 \in \RR{}[x]$, we are not thinking of $x$ as a real number; $x^2 + 1$ is a symbolic expression. However, we *can* evaluate a polynomial at any element of $k$, or of any field $K$ containing $k$: given $f = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n$ and $r \in K$, we set $f(r) = a_0 + a_1 r + \cdots + a_n r^n \in K$. Comparing with the product formula shows $(f + g)(r) = f(r) + g(r)$ and $(fg)(r) = f(r)g(r)$, so evaluation at $r$ is a ring homomorphism $k[x] \to K$.
:::

:::definition{4.3.2} Degree
The ***degree*** $\deg f$ of a nonzero polynomial $f = \sum a_i x^i$ is the largest $n$ with $a_n \neq 0$, and $a_n$ is its ***leading coefficient***. The polynomial is ***monic*** if its leading coefficient is $1$. Nonzero constants have degree $0$; by convention $\deg 0 = -\infty$.
:::

:::lemma{4.3.3} Degree of a product
If $f, g \in k[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg \neq 0$ and $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$. In particular, $k[x]$ has no zero divisors.
:::

:::proof
Write $f = \sum_{i \leq m} a_i x^i$ and $g = \sum_{j \leq n} b_j x^j$ with $a_m \neq 0$ and $b_n \neq 0$. In the coefficient $c_l = \sum_{i + j = l} a_i b_j$ of $fg$, every term with $i > m$ or $j > n$ vanishes. If $l > m + n$, every pair with $i + j = l$ has $i > m$ or $j > n$, so $c_l = 0$. For $l = m + n$, the only surviving term is $c_{m+n} = a_m b_n$, which is nonzero because $k$ has no zero divisors.
:::

:::proposition{4.3.4} Units of $k[x]$
The units of $k[x]$ are exactly the nonzero constants. In particular, $k[x]$ is not a field.
:::

:::proof
A nonzero constant $c$ has inverse $c^{-1}$. Conversely, if $fg = 1$, then $f, g \neq 0$ and $\deg f + \deg g = \deg 1 = 0$ by the lemma. Both degrees are nonnegative, so $\deg f = 0$ and $f$ is a nonzero constant. For instance, $x$ has no inverse in $k[x]$.
:::

## <span class="num">4.3.2</span> The Field of Rational Functions

To make $k[x]$ into a field we allow fractions of polynomials, just as we pass from $\ZZ$ to $\QQ$.

:::definition{4.3.5} Field of rational functions
The ***field of rational functions*** over $k$ is $$k(x) \coloneqq \left\{\frac{p}{q} \;\middle|\; p, q \in k[x], \, q \neq 0 \right\}\bigg/\sim, \qquad \text{where } \frac{p}{q} \sim \frac{p'}{q'} \text{ iff } pq' = p'q.$$ Addition and multiplication are defined as for ordinary fractions: $$\frac{p}{q} + \frac{p'}{q'} = \frac{pq' + p'q}{qq'}, \qquad \frac{p}{q} \cdot \frac{p'}{q'} = \frac{pp'}{qq'}.$$
:::

The denominators $qq'$ are nonzero by Lemma [4.3.3](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#lemma-4-3-3). As for $\QQ$, one checks that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation (transitivity uses cancellation in $k[x]$, which holds because $k[x]$ has no zero divisors), that the operations do not depend on the chosen representatives, and that the ring axioms hold. The inverse of a nonzero element $p/q$ is $q/p$, so $k(x)$ is a field. Identifying $p$ with $p/1$ makes $k[x]$ a subring of $k(x)$.

This construction generalizes to polynomials in any number of variables, giving the field $k(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ of rational functions in $n$ variables.

## <span class="num">4.3.3</span> Formal Power Series

Another way to extend $k[x]$ is to allow *infinite* sums.

:::definition{4.3.6} Formal power series
The ***ring of formal power series*** over $k$ is $$k\llbracket x \rrbracket \coloneqq \left\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} a_i x^i \;\middle|\; a_i \in k \right\}.$$ Addition is coefficientwise, and multiplication is given by the same formula as for polynomials: for $f = \sum a_i x^i$ and $g = \sum b_i x^i$, we set $fg = \sum c_n x^n$ with $c_n = \sum_{i+j=n} a_i b_j$.
:::

:::note
The product formula makes sense because each coefficient $c_n$ is a *finite* sum: only the $n + 1$ pairs $(i, j) = (0, n), \ldots, (n, 0)$ satisfy $i + j = n$ with $i, j \geq 0$. This is why these power series are called “formal”: no question of convergence arises. The ring axioms are checked as for $k[x]$, and $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ contains $k[x]$ as a subring (polynomials are the power series with only finitely many nonzero coefficients).
:::

Unlike $k[x]$, the ring $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has many units.

:::lemma{4.3.7} Units of $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$
A power series $f = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} a_i x^i \in k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has a multiplicative inverse if and only if $a_0 \neq 0$.
:::

:::proof
($\Rightarrow$) If $fg = 1$ for some $g = \sum b_i x^i$, then comparing constant terms gives $a_0 b_0 = 1$, so $a_0 \neq 0$.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume $a_0 \neq 0$. We construct $g = \sum b_i x^i$ with $fg = 1$ one coefficient at a time. The constant term of $fg$ must be $a_0 b_0 = 1$, so we take $b_0 = a_0^{-1}$. For $n \geq 1$, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $fg$ must vanish: $$a_0 b_n + \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_{n-i} = 0, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad b_n = -a_0^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_{n-i}.$$ The right side involves only $b_0, \ldots, b_{n-1}$, so these equations determine $b_1, b_2, \ldots$ inductively, and the resulting $g$ satisfies $fg = 1$.
:::

:::example{4.3.8}
The geometric series: in $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ we have $(1 - x)^{-1} = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + \cdots = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} x^i$. Indeed, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1 - x)\sum_{i \geq 0} x^i$ is $1 - 1 = 0$ for $n \geq 1$, and the constant term is $1$.
:::

## <span class="num">4.3.4</span> Laurent Series

Every nonzero element of $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ can be written as $x^m(a_m + a_{m+1}x + \cdots)$, where $a_m$ is its first nonzero coefficient. The second factor is a unit by Lemma [4.3.7](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#lemma-4-3-7), so to obtain a field we need only invert $x$, that is, allow finitely many negative powers of $x$.

:::definition{4.3.9} Field of Laurent series
The ***field of Laurent series*** over $k$ is $$k(\!(x)\!) \coloneqq \left\{\sum_{i=m}^{\infty} a_i x^i \;\middle|\; m \in \ZZ, \, a_i \in k \right\},$$ the set of formal series in which only finitely many negative powers of $x$ appear. Addition is coefficientwise and multiplication is again $\big(\sum a_i x^i\big)\big(\sum b_j x^j\big) = \sum c_n x^n$ with $c_n = \sum_{i + j = n} a_i b_j$.
:::

If $a_i = 0$ for $i < m$ and $b_j = 0$ for $j < m'$, the sum defining $c_n$ runs only over $m \leq i \leq n - m'$, a finite range, and $c_n = 0$ for $n < m + m'$; so the product is again a Laurent series. As for $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$, this makes $k(\!(x)\!)$ a commutative ring containing $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ as a subring.

:::proposition{4.3.10} $k(\!(x)\!)$ is a field
Every nonzero Laurent series has a multiplicative inverse.
:::

:::proof
Let $f = \sum_{i=m}^{\infty} a_i x^i$ with $a_m \neq 0$. Then $f = x^m g$, where $g = a_m + a_{m+1}x + \cdots \in k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has nonzero constant term. By Lemma [4.3.7](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#lemma-4-3-7), $g$ has an inverse $g^{-1}$ in $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$. Then $f^{-1} = x^{-m} g^{-1} \in k(\!(x)\!)$.
:::

## <span class="num">4.3.5</span> Roots of Polynomials and Field Extensions

Given a polynomial $f \in k[x]$ with $\deg f \geq 1$, we can ask whether $f$ has a root in $k$, and if not, whether we can *extend* $k$ to a larger field containing one.

:::definition{4.3.11} Root
Let $K$ be a field extension of $k$ and $f \in k[x]$. An element $r \in K$ is a ***root*** of $f$ if $f(r) = 0$. We write $K/k$ for the extension and sometimes $k \subseteq K$.
:::

:::example{4.3.12}
The polynomial $x^2 - 2 \in \QQ{}[x]$ has no roots in $\QQ$, since $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. Consider $$\QQ(\sqrt{2}) = \{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \in \QQ\} \subseteq \RR.$$ It contains $\QQ$ and the root $\sqrt{2}$ of $x^2 - 2$, and it is closed under addition and under multiplication, since $(a + b\sqrt{2})(c + d\sqrt{2}) = (ac + 2bd) + (ad + bc)\sqrt{2}$. It is also closed under inverses: for $a + b\sqrt{2} \neq 0$, $$\frac{1}{a + b\sqrt{2}} = \frac{a - b\sqrt{2}}{a^2 - 2b^2} = \frac{a}{a^2 - 2b^2} - \frac{b}{a^2 - 2b^2}\sqrt{2} \in \QQ(\sqrt{2}).$$ Here $a^2 - 2b^2 \neq 0$: if $b \neq 0$, then $a^2 = 2b^2$ would give $\sqrt{2} = |a/b| \in \QQ$, and if $b = 0$, then $a \neq 0$. So $\QQ(\sqrt{2})$ is a subfield of $\RR$, and a field extension of $\QQ$ containing a root of $x^2 - 2$.
:::

:::example{4.3.13}
Similarly, $x^2 + 1 \in \RR{}[x]$ has no real roots. The extension $$\RR(i) = \RR(\sqrt{-1}) = \{a + bi : a, b \in \RR\} = \CC$$ is the field of complex numbers, which contains the roots $\pm i$ of $x^2 + 1$.
:::

:::lemma{4.3.14} Factor theorem
Let $f \in k[x]$ have degree $n \geq 1$ and let $r \in k$. Then $f = (x - r)q + f(r)$ for some $q \in k[x]$ of degree $n - 1$. In particular, $r$ is a root of $f$ if and only if $f = (x - r)q$ for some $q \in k[x]$.
:::

:::proof
For $i \geq 1$ we have $x^i - r^i = (x - r)(x^{i-1} + r x^{i-2} + \cdots + r^{i-1})$. If $f = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i$, then $$f - f(r) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i (x^i - r^i) = (x - r)q, \qquad q = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i (x^{i-1} + r x^{i-2} + \cdots + r^{i-1}),$$ and the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $q$ is $a_n \neq 0$. If $f(r) = 0$ this gives $f = (x - r)q$. Conversely, if $f = (x - r)q$, evaluating at $r$ gives $f(r) = 0 \cdot q(r) = 0$.
:::

:::corollary{4.3.15} Number of roots
A nonzero polynomial $f \in k[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ roots in $k$.
:::

:::proof
By induction on $n$. A nonzero constant has no roots. Let $n \geq 1$. If $f$ has no root we are done. Otherwise let $r$ be a root and write $f = (x - r)q$ with $\deg q = n - 1$. If $s \neq r$ is another root, then $0 = f(s) = (s - r)q(s)$ with $s - r \neq 0$, so $q(s) = 0$. Thus every root of $f$ other than $r$ is a root of $q$, and $q$ has at most $n - 1$ roots by induction.
:::

:::definition{4.3.16} Algebraically closed field
A field $k$ is ***algebraically closed*** if every non-constant polynomial $f \in k[x]$ has a root in $k$.
:::

:::proposition{4.3.17} Factorization into linear factors
A field $k$ is algebraically closed if and only if every polynomial $f \in k[x]$ of degree $n \geq 1$ factors as $$f = c(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\cdots(x - r_n), \qquad c \in k \setminus \{0\}, \; r_1, \ldots, r_n \in k$$ (the $r_i$ need not be distinct).
:::

:::proof
If every such $f$ factors in this way, then $r_1$ is a root of $f$, so $k$ is algebraically closed. Conversely, let $k$ be algebraically closed; we induct on $n$. If $n = 1$, then $f = a_1 x + a_0 = a_1\big(x - (-a_0 a_1^{-1})\big)$. If $n > 1$, let $r_1$ be a root of $f$. By the factor theorem, $f = (x - r_1)q$ with $\deg q = n - 1 \geq 1$, and by induction $q = c(x - r_2)\cdots(x - r_n)$.
:::

:::note
The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra states that $\CC$ is algebraically closed; we do not prove it here. Over an algebraically closed field, every non-constant polynomial already has a root, so adjoining roots of polynomials produces no larger fields. The field $\CC$ is called the *algebraic closure* of $\RR$: it is algebraically closed, and every element of $\CC$ is a root of a nonzero real polynomial ($a + bi$ is a root of $x^2 - 2ax + a^2 + b^2$). By contrast, $\QQ$ is very far from algebraically closed: $x^2 - 2$, $x^2 - 3$, $x^3 - 2$, … have no rational roots, and adjoining their roots gives infinitely many different extensions of $\QQ$.
:::
